newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Minister says Berre refinery talks blocked.
newsitem.headline: French Minister says Berre refinery talks blocked.

text.p: French Industry Minister Franck Borotra said in an interview with the Les Echos newspaper on Friday that oil industry talks abour restructuring refineries at the Berre lake near Marseille seemed to have stalled.

However, commenting on Shell's recent announcement that it planned to cut capacity at its Berre refinery, Borotra said this was a "minimum" and he hoped it would not be an obstacle to further talks aimed at a wider agreement with competitors.

"A discussion has been opened, at their initiative, between Shell, BP and Total to see how they could restructure, with the minimum of social consequences and the maximum of industrial efficiency, the refinery capacity on the lake of Berre," Borotra said.

"The idea was to satisfy both the demand for refined products in the area and the petrochemical needs of these large companies," he added. "It seems that these negotiations are today blocked," Borotra added.
But company spokeswomen said thet talks were not dead.
"I do not think that they are blocked. We are ready to resume talks after the Shell announcement, which we welcome," said a spokeswoman at Total.
At Shell France, a spokeswoman said the company had been forced to make its unilateral closure decision after talks with the others provided inconclusive.

"We have not been able to find a solution in discussions with the other companies and this has led us to announce our decision last week. We are waiting for approval from the Industry Ministry," the Shell spokeswoman said.
But she added that "the door remains open" to further talks with the other companies.
At BP France there was no immediate reaction.
Shell has also been in talks with Esso France, which operates the 107,000 barrels per day (bpd) Fos refinery.

Shell on announced on February 8 it planned to cut its capacity at 127,000 bpd Berre and said it had sought formal approval to reduce crude throughput to 3.5 million tonnes per year from 6.5 million and shut one of its two catcrackers.
"Shell has announced, starting 1998, the closure of part of its refining capacity, in particular one cracker -- we do not exactly know which one -- and associated units," Borotra said.
"I believe this announcement is a minimum and I hope it will not be an obstacle to the continuation of negotiations on a much wider agreement with the two other oil groups," he added.
He said that BP had not yet notified his ministry of any plans to sell its 199,000 bpd refinery at Lavera.

"The rentability of the industrial complex (at Lavera) is a problem for the owner of today as well as for the buyer of tomorrow. The question of the organisation of refining in that area in relation to the market is an unavoidable element."
Total chairman Thierry Desmarest has recently been quoted in newspapers as saying Shell should bear the brunt of the costs of any restructuring in the area.

Desmarest told Total's January 31 annual results news conference that his company was willing to participate in a resturcturing but because Total's refineries -- including the 127,000 bpd one at La Med near Marseille -- were above average efficient, he did not plan to shut any of them but was willing to give other oil groups access to the capacity.
Borotra said on Friday that there was an overcapacity in European refinery of 10 percent and the closure of some 10 refineries was needed.

"As Minister of Industry, it is my task to see that the French refining industry is not paying the highest price for the restructuring. Secondly, it is a problem for the capacity of the Mediterranean refineries, not just those of the lake of Berre," Borotra said.

Berre, Lavera, La Med and Fos are four main refining sites around a small inland lake near Marseille in the south of France with industry experts saying the area has the biggest overcapacity of Europe.
